# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is lazy. Left to itself, it sits still, and when it does move, it only moves downhill. Everything about a municipal water system is, in one way or another, a scheme for overcoming this laziness—storing water high, pushing it with pumps, and managing the physics of elevation so that a tenant on the 40th floor can take a shower at 7 a.m. with the same ease as a homeowner at the base of a hill. To understand how this works, it helps to follow a single drop through a concrete example.

## The Fundamental Currency: Head

Engineers describe water pressure in terms of "head"—the height of a column of water. Every 10 meters (roughly 33 feet) of elevation corresponds to about one atmosphere of pressure, or about 14.7 pounds per square inch. This single fact dominates everything else. If a reservoir sits 100 meters above a faucet, the water arriving at that faucet carries about ten atmospheres of pressure, minus whatever friction losses occur along the pipes.
